newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST-US Nov retail sales to show moderate gain.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-US Nov retail sales to show moderate gain.

text.p: November retail sales data will show moderate growth that does not reflect apparently brisk holiday shopping, U.S. analysts said, noting that the Thanksgiving holiday fell later than usual this year.

Less autos, the average forecast of economists surveyed said retail sales grew by 0.2 percent. Economists' forecasts for an ex-auto number ranged from down 0.1 percent to up 0.7 percent because of uncertainty over measures, economists said.
The U.S. Commerce Department has the data slated for release at 0830 EST/1330 on Thursday, December 12.

The late Thanksgiving holiday may have curbed holiday spending in November, holding the stuffing from retailers' pockets past the cut-off for government data collection. With that said, James Padhina, economist at MMS International, underscored that recent growth in savings and income otherwise would suggest a bias to the upside.

"Sometimes those are signs people are laying off big ticket items this late in an expansion, but it also indicated to us that people may have been just taking a breather from the breakneck pace in the first half of the year," Padhina said.

He noted that retail sales data in 12 of the last 14 years have exceeded market expectations by an average of 0.7 percent. But because of of data collection quirks and the recent consumer tendency to hold out for better bargains, Padhina said the number may indeed still print at plus 0.3 percent, in line with the latest Reuters survey.

John Ryding, senior economist at Bear, Stearns & Co, also suggested the data should paint a picture of moderate growth as expected for the fourth quarter -- but perhaps not an entirely representative one given the late Thanksgiving and the latest entries of related data.

Specifically, the BTM/Schroders Weekly Chain Store Sales Index rose 1.0 percent in first week of December. And Telecheck Services, which Ryding said tends to underestimate sales given the rising use of credit cards, on Tuesday said same-store retail sales rose 3.7 percent for the first 10 days of the holiday shopping period.

Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette Securities Money Market Economist Marilyn Schaja shied away from making conclusions about recent data, which she said should not affect an expected 0.2 percent to 0.3 percent rise in November sales.

"Even the Johnson Redbook number, (up 0.8 percent in the first week of December) follows a decline of 0.7 percent for the whole of November," Schaja said. "You're back essentially to where you were in October, so I wouldn't say that's great."
Whether better retail sales are reflected in November's or December's data, Ryding contends they will show the economy is in good shape and rising above its third quarter performance.
"I think we're looking at 2.5 percent (gross domestic product growth) in the fourth quarter in real terms," Ryding said, a figure entrenched between Q3 and the first half.

A larger than expected number of 0.6 percent to 0.7 percent would likely push U.S. Treasury yields up a few basis points, he said. The recent backup to the 6.50 percent level will temper the reaction to strength, however.
